skill.name: tool-design
skill.description: Guides the design, documentation, consolidation, and evaluation of tools for AI agents and MCP-based workflows.
skill.summary: Design clearer agent tools with better descriptions, naming, errors, and workflow boundaries.
skill.author: ChakshuGautam

security_audit.summary: Most static matches are false positives from Markdown code fences, prose, and illustrative templates. Two external command examples are confirmed because they pass agent-supplied command strings to sandbox.exec(). No prompt injection, data exfiltration intent, or unauthorized network behavior was found.

remediation.suggestion: Make sandbox isolation, command allowlists, timeouts, read-only mounts, and no host filesystem access mandatory in the guidance.
Add a checklist for cases where command execution tools are forbidden, including secrets, production data, compliance workflows, and write access.

remediation.issue: Illustrative snippets may be copied into production
remediation.suggestion: Label snippets as examples and show safer wrappers around sandbox.exec with validation, logging, and resource limits.

content.user_title: Design Agent Tools That Models Use Correctly
content.value_statement: Agent tools fail when descriptions, parameters, and errors leave choices ambiguous. This skill gives practical patterns for clearer contracts, smaller tool sets, and recoverable failures.
actual_capabilities: Explains how to write tool descriptions that cover purpose, timing, inputs, outputs, and errors.
Provides naming and parameter conventions for consistent agent-facing tool APIs.
Shows when to consolidate related tools into one workflow-level tool.
Describes response format options for concise and detailed tool outputs.
Gives evaluation criteria for clarity, completeness, recoverability, efficiency, and consistency.
Includes examples of strong and weak tool descriptions.
limitations: It does not build, deploy, or run MCP servers for you.
Example code is illustrative and requires production hardening.
Architectural reduction guidance depends on strong sandboxing and clear documentation.
It does not validate security controls in your environment.

use_cases.title: Design a New Agent Tool
use_cases.description: Create a tool contract with clear triggers, parameter names, return formats, and recovery-focused errors.

use_cases.title: Reduce Tool Selection Confusion
use_cases.description: Review overlapping tools and decide where consolidation or namespacing will improve agent choices.

use_cases.title: Improve Tool Documentation Quality
use_cases.description: Audit descriptions, examples, and error messages before exposing tools to Claude, Codex, or Claude Code.

prompt_templates.title: Draft a Basic Tool Description
prompt_templates.scenario: Beginner: create one clear tool contract.
prompt_templates.prompt: Use the tool-design skill to draft a description for a tool named [tool name]. Include when to use it, parameters, returns, and errors.

prompt_templates.title: Review Tool Clarity
prompt_templates.scenario: Intermediate: find ambiguity in an existing tool.
prompt_templates.prompt: Use the tool-design skill to review this tool description for clarity, completeness, recoverability, efficiency, and consistency: [paste description].

prompt_templates.title: Consolidate a Tool Set
prompt_templates.prompt: Use the tool-design skill to analyze these tools and recommend which should be merged, separated, or namespaced: [list tools and purposes].

prompt_templates.title: Design an Evaluation Plan
prompt_templates.scenario: Advanced: test agent tool behavior before launch.
prompt_templates.prompt: Use the tool-design skill to create an evaluation plan for these agent tools. Include representative tasks, expected calls, failure modes, and improvement steps.

output_examples.input: Review a customer lookup tool with vague parameters and generic errors.
output_examples.output: The response identifies ambiguous parameters, missing return details, weak error recovery, and revised wording for agent-facing use.

output_examples.input: Decide whether five scheduling tools should stay separate.
output_examples.output: The response groups sequential scheduling steps into one workflow tool and keeps unrelated administrative actions separate.

output_examples.input: Create a pre-launch checklist for MCP tool descriptions.
output_examples.output: The response lists checks for fully qualified names, parameter consistency, examples, return formats, and actionable errors.

best_practices: Write every tool description to answer what it does, when to use it, what it accepts, and what it returns.
Use consistent names, formats, and error structures across related tools.
Test tool designs with realistic agent requests and refine descriptions from observed failures.
anti_patterns: Do not expose vague tools that force agents to guess the target system, query format, or result shape.
Do not split one user workflow across many overlapping tools without a clear selection rule.
Do not use broad command execution patterns without sandboxing, validation, and explicit safety limits.

faq.question: What does this skill help me design?
faq.answer: It helps design agent-facing tools, descriptions, parameters, return formats, error messages, and tool collections.

faq.question: Does it generate production-ready tool code?
faq.answer: No. It provides design guidance and examples that need implementation, testing, and security review.

faq.question: Can it help with MCP tool names?
faq.answer: Yes. It recommends fully qualified MCP tool names so agents can select tools reliably.

faq.question: When should I consolidate tools?
faq.answer: Consolidate tools when they represent sequential steps in one workflow and separate selection creates agent confusion.

faq.question: When should tools stay separate?
faq.answer: Keep tools separate when they have different behaviors, safety boundaries, users, or independent use cases.

faq.question: Is the architectural reduction guidance always safe?
faq.answer: No. Command execution and file system access require strict sandboxing, permissions, monitoring, and environment-specific security review.
